name: Biafine

lead: Biafine is a water-based, non-greasy emulsion cream developed and sold mainly in France, where it is a pharmacy staple for first- and second-degree burns including sunburn, superficial wounds and redness after radiotherapy. Its active ingredient is trolamine (triethanolamine).

For looks, skincare fans use it to soothe irritated skin and support recovery after sun exposure or cosmetic procedures, with the aim of calmer, less red skin. Clinical research is concentrated in radiation dermatitis, where trials have compared it with other creams, films and standard care, with mixed results.

paras: It is applied as a cream to the affected skin. Users describe a cooling, milky, non-greasy layer that absorbs easily. In France it is sold without a prescription in tubes; elsewhere people obtain it through personal importation or buy a similarly named wound-dressing product. It is not a sunscreen.

It is intended for non-infected skin; label guidance says to seek medical advice if symptoms persist. Grokipedia lists excipients including propylene glycol, parabens and fragrance, which can matter to people with sensitivities. It is not FDA-approved in the US as a medication.

angle.text: People apply Biafine to sunburnt, irritated or freshly treated skin to soothe it and support healing, so the skin looks calmer and less red as it recovers.

lead: Biafine is a topical oil-in-water emulsion with trolamine as its active ingredient, developed and primarily marketed in France for the symptomatic treatment of first- and second-degree burns including sunburn, non-infected superficial wounds, and redness (erythema) secondary to radiotherapy[1]. It has long been a fixture of French pharmacies and has a following among skincare enthusiasts for minor irritation and post-procedure recovery[1].

The appearance link is skin recovery. A product that keeps skin moist and calms inflammation after sunburn, a peel or a minor wound is used to help the area heal with less visible redness. Grokipedia describes the emulsion as providing a moist environment for natural healing and as non-comedogenic and steroid-free[1].

Most clinical work has been in oncology. Randomised trials in breast cancer patients having radiotherapy compared Biafine with other agents or no treatment for preventing radiation dermatitis[2][3][4]. A 2007 review summarised its use for wound healing[5].
infobox: OTC in France; not FDA-approved as a drug in US

paras: Cosmetic and appearance uses: skincare communities use it for sunburn and minor irritation and for recovery after procedures, drawing on its reputation as a soothing, non-comedogenic cream[1].
Medical uses: minor burns, superficial wounds and radiotherapy-related redness in France[1].
Grokipedia lists trolamine at 0.670 g per 100 g of emulsion, with emulsifiers and stabilisers, paraffins, perhydrosqualene, avocado oil, propylene glycol, preservatives, fragrance and water[1].

It is sold without prescription in France. Grokipedia states that it is not FDA-approved as a medication in the US, personal importation is generally permitted in limited quantities, and a similarly named emulsion has FDA 510(k) clearance as a wound dressing device marketed by Bausch Health[1].
In mice, Biafine accelerated excisional and burn wound healing[6]. A 1997 study in human epidermal wounds found it was chemotactic for macrophages and raised the IL-1/IL-6 ratio[7].

A multicentre randomised trial in 74 women receiving breast radiotherapy compared Biafine, Lipiderm and no treatment; it found no statistically significant advantage over the control arm on the maximal treatment level required, although 86 percent of patients in both treated arms expressed a favourable opinion[2]. The RTOG 97-13 phase III trial compared Biafine with best supportive care in women having breast irradiation[3], and a phase II study examined it with concomitant chemotherapy[4]. A randomised intra-patient trial in head and neck cancer found Mepitel Film superior to Biafine[8], and a phase III trial compared Mebo ointment with Biafine in breast radiotherapy[9]. A trial studied a trolamine emulsion after shave biopsy[10]. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of preventive topical agents for radiation dermatitis provide wider context[11][12].
